logp.method_description: Partition coefficient is a parameter that determines how a solute substance is distributed between two phases, i.e., polar and nonpolar phases. In partition coefficient experiment, the polar phase is considered to be water and nonpolar phase is n-octanol which has two heads: (i) a long lipophilic alkyl chain (R) and (ii) a polar hydroxyl (OH) group. This structure of n-octanol resembles the lipid molecules (phospholipids and sterols) of cell membrane. So, octanol–water partition coefficient (log P) best represents the tendency of a given compound such as drug to pass across the cell membrane. In this study, the log P of [Pd(1, 3-pn)(acac)]Cl complex was measured by a shake-flask technique in a mixture of doubly distilled water and n-octanol (Manojkumar et al. 2019). Palladium(II) complex (0.002 g) was dissolved in a mixture of doubly distilled water and n-octanol (5 mL of each) and shaken without interruption overnight. It was then allowed to stand (without stirring) for one hour until phase separation occurred. After, the water and octanol phases were carefully separated with two different syringes. UV–Vis spectroscopy and Beer-Lambert law were utilized to determine the metal complex concentration in each phase. Eventually, the following equation was used to estimate the lipophilicity (log P) value of [Pd(1, 3-pn)(acac)]Cl complex: logP = log(Co/Cw), where CO and CW are the concentrations of complex in the octanol and aqueous phases, respectively.
